note_6.reason: Explains specific barrier and ceramide differences around the eye area, providing clear consumer education value.
note_6.draft:
The skin around the human eye - the periorbital region - is approximately 0.5 millimetres thick. On the rest of the face, the dermis and epidermis together average between 1.5 and 2 millimetres.

I want to explain why that structural difference matters, because we are asked almost weekly whether an eye cream is genuinely necessary or simply a facial moisturiser repackaged in a 15-millilitre tube.

I'm not saying the cosmetic industry has never exploited the category with identical formulations and higher margins. I'm saying periorbital skin has a fundamentally different barrier architecture, and treating it as identical to the rest of the face frequently causes avoidable barrier disruption.

Here is why the mechanism changes:

First, periorbital skin contains far fewer sebaceous glands and a markedly lower baseline content of intercellular lipids, particularly ceramides. Its capacity to maintain barrier integrity against external stressors is naturally lower, and its rate of transepidermal water loss is consistently higher.

Second, because the stratum corneum is so thin in this zone, molecular penetration happens considerably faster. A vehicle system or surfactant concentration engineered to deliver actives through the thicker epidermis of the cheeks will deliver those same compounds far more aggressively to periorbital tissue. 

The formulation does not change. The barrier does. The result is contact dermatitis and sensitisation from a product your forehead tolerated without incident.

Skinstinct does not manufacture a separate eye cream. Making that formulation decision meant being clear with customers that our standard facial moisturisers should not simply be swept right up to the lower eyelid as a convenience.

If you choose to use your regular moisturiser around your eyes, check the INCI list first. If the formula contains high concentrations of penetration enhancers, synthetic fragrance, exfoliating acids, or retinoids, keep application outside the orbital rim - the bone you can feel beneath the eye - rather than bringing it onto the thin skin of the lid itself.
